<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Robotic‐arm assisted systems are increasingly used for knee arthroplasty, however introduction of new systems can involve a learning curve. We aimed to define the learning curve in terms of operative time and component placement/sizing of a robotic system for total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in a team of experienced surgeons, and to investigate mid‐term patient outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 101 consecutive patients underwent primary robotic‐arm assisted TKA by three surgeons (mean 2 year follow‐up). Operative times, component placement, implant sizing and reoperations were recorded. Cumulative Summation (CUSUM) was used to analyse learning curves. Patient outcomes were compared between learning and proficiency phases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The learning curve was 16 cases, with a 12‐min increase in operative time (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.01). Once proficiency was achieved, the greatest time reductions were seen for navigation registration (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.003) and bone preparation (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.0001). A learning curve was found with polyethylene (PE) insert sizing (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.01). No differences were found between learning and proficiency groups in terms of implant survival (100% and 97%, respectively, NS) or patient‐reported outcome measures at 2 years (NS).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Introduction of a robotic‐arm assisted system for TKA led to increased operative times for navigation registration and bone preparation, and a learning curve with PE insert sizing. No difference in patient outcomes between learning and proficiency groups at 2 years was found. These findings can inform surgeons' expectations when starting to use robotic‐assisted systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Robotic‐arm assisted total knee arthroplasty has a learning curve of 16 cases and increased operative time of 12 min
